{"id": "6:77/q12", "question": "What is Abraham asking for in لَئِن لَّمْ يَهْدِنِى رَبِّى?", "turns_on": "Whether Abraham is seeking initial truth, preservation of guidance already possessed, or addressing the worshippers by conditional example; Islahi disputes making the condition past.", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q12/p1", "position": "Continued, increased or firm guidance already possessed.", "reasons": "Tustarī and Sahl seek uninterrupted establishment; Sahl says without God's help Abraham could fall into his people's error. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ calls it increased guidance after distinguishing Abraham from his people. Wāḥidī, Baghawī and Ibn al-Jawzī compare Abraham's prayer in 14:35 that he and his children avoid idols; Qurṭubī compares 1:6. Sulamī's unnamed transmitters ask increase, firmness and protection against worship like the people; al-Wāsiṭī fears return to his own attributes. Qurṭubī cites Shuʿayb's conditional return in 7:89 as a rational possibility. Islahi says the conditional is a general truth and rejects shifting it into the past."}, {"id": "6:77/q12/p2", "position": "Divine aid to attain or recognize the true Lord and affirm His unity.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says guidance enables the truth of tawḥīd; Bayḍāwī calls it aid to attain truth; Ālūsī glosses the inescapable path since none of the observed bodies can be God. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says yahdinī plainly means 'guide me' and supports a childhood episode; Ibn Jarīr, as reported by Ibn Kathīr, takes the request as evidence for contemplation. Ālūsī reports a request for help finding truth but finds this reading remote from the apparent sense; he nevertheless says certainty acquired through reasoning can coexist with debate."}, {"id": "6:77/q12/p3", "position": "A fair-minded conditional warning to moon worshippers about their own straying.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, transmitted by Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī, says anyone deifying the setting moon is astray. Bayḍāwī and Nasafī say Abraham guides his people through the example; Bursevī says the plea indirectly names their error; Ibn al-Munīr calls it stronger than the earlier 'I do not love those that set.' Biqāʿī and Ālūsī see a tactful, escalating repudiation, the first proof having softened resistance before explicit disavowal in 6:78. Elmalılı and Ṭabāṭabāʾī treat the conditional as a hypothetical of what persistence in moon worship would mean. Islahi calls it a mirror held to the people."}, {"id": "6:77/q12/p4", "position": "The condition refers to a past absence of guidance.", "reasons": "Islahi reports this interpretation only to reject it as an unnecessary strain on the wording."}]}
{"id": "6:77/q13", "question": "What does the conditional plea teach about the source of guidance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q13/p1", "position": "Only God grants effective guidance; displayed proofs and human reasoning alone do not supply it.", "reasons": "Rāzī says enabling, obstacle removal and presentation of proofs were already present, so the requested guidance goes beyond them; he adduces 26:78 and 14:35. Biqāʿī likewise excludes other agents, mere displayed proof and already possessed inferential knowledge. Bayḍāwī says truth requires divine enabling; al-Wāsiṭī says a servant supplies the invocation but God supplies guidance. Tustarī, Elmalılı, Islahi and Study Quran stress reliance on divine guidance; Islahi describes revelation as 'light upon light' with 24:35. Al-Zamakhsharī's reported warning also depends on God's enabling grace."}]}
{"id": "6:77/q14", "question": "How is لَئِن ... لَأَكُونَنَّ constructed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q14/p1", "position": "The first lām marks an oath; the second introduces its answer.", "reasons": "Jishumī identifies these respective functions in Abraham's conditional statement."}]}
{"id": "6:77/q15", "question": "Who are ٱلْقَوْمِ ٱلضَّآلِّينَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q15/p1", "position": "People who miss true guidance by worshipping created beings, especially the moon, stars or idols.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī names worshippers of anyone besides God; Baghawī glosses distance from guidance; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says idolaters and worshippers of created things are intended, although 'astray' is broader. Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Bursevī and al-Zamakhsharī apply the warning to the moon's worshippers. Al-Suddī reports Abraham's plea after the moon's disappearance; Study Quran says it may expose his people's religious status."}]}
{"id": "6:77/q16", "question": "How do inward readings understand the moon and Abraham's guidance?", "turns_on": "Which inner faculty or spiritual passage the celestial sequence signifies.", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q16/p1", "position": "The moon is the illuminated heart; its setting discloses dependence on the spirit, and guidance passes beyond luminous inner veils to divine light.", "reasons": "Qāshānī places the heart above the soul, illuminated by disclosures through the names al-ʿAlīm and al-Ḥakīm; its light is borrowed from the spirit and may be obscured by the soul. He likens stopping at such luminous veils to Christians' error."}, {"id": "6:77/q16/p2", "position": "The sequence depicts passage from human faculties and darkness toward subsistence and direct realization in God.", "reasons": "Sulamī reports movement from compulsion through lordship's and awe's lights, effacement of human traits and subsistence in the Everlasting. Qushayrī says gnosis removes seeking and doubt; another account moves from seeing signs through God, to seeing them as God's, to seeing them effaced in God. Rāzī reports mapping star, moon and sun to sense, imagination/estimation and intellect, all finite and governed. Tustarī says Abraham's path is generosity and disavowal of all but God; the Gabriel episode illustrates reliance on God alone. Al-Wāsiṭī says looking at one's own attributes risks misguidance."}]}
{"id": "6:77/q17", "question": "How does the moon scene fit Abraham's argument and the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is the immediate progression of Abraham's argument or its place in the sūra's prophetic message.", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q17/p1", "position": "It continues the signs shown to Abraham and advances his gradual refutation of worshipped celestial bodies.", "reasons": "Jishumī links the narrative to 6:75's signs and Abraham's reasoning. Wāḥidī says the moon and sun repeat the star's argument. Biqāʿī says the earlier setting prepared the audience; Ālūsī says resistance softened before the stronger insinuation here and disavowal at 6:78. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says guidance increases once proof is established. Islahi says this expands the prior brief statement that heavenly bodies obey divine law; Abraham had first addressed his father, then his nation, and 6:79–80 speaks with prophetic authority. Ṭabāṭabāʾī likewise places the astral test after debate with father and idol worshippers."}, {"id": "6:77/q17/p2", "position": "The account grounds the sūra's call to Muhammad in the shared monotheistic mission of Abraham and the prophets.", "reasons": "Islahi says Muhammad follows earlier prophets' guidance, preaches without compelling belief, and revives Abraham's religion for Israelites and Ishmaelites who claimed him while inheriting later fabrications. He says prophets share a mission but adapt their speech: John and Jesus use parables, while Abraham's combative audience required gradual reasoning, double meaning and even gentle humor. Kuryolu says the Qur'an chiefly confronts corrupted innate divinity through shirk; Abraham's hanif confession culminates in worship of the Creator alone."}]}
{"id": "6:77/q18", "question": "What further lesson is drawn from Abraham's observation of the heavenly bodies?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q18/p1", "position": "Observing their dependence directs worship and love to their Creator and warns against idolatry.", "reasons": "Islahi says fading objects cannot merit the Creator's love, the moon scene makes such worship a grave and sorrowful error, and reason and innate capacity can move people beyond man-made idols. Kuryolu says Abraham's observation establishes the proper faith in God and the Qur'an confronts polytheism as corruption of an innate sense of divinity. Elmalılı notes the moon's beauty can seduce without divine guidance."}, {"id": "6:77/q18/p2", "position": "The eastward location of rising signs and westward setting connect this scene to reported directions of trial and repentance.", "reasons": "Burhān cites the Prophet's report that fitna and disbelief come from the east and the door of repentance opens from the west, and attaches it to Abraham's rejection of setting stars."}]}
{"id": "6:77/q19", "question": "What exegetical sciences are catalogued alongside this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q19/p1", "position": "The reported catalog covers revelation contexts, transmission and readings, and recitation practice within a broader scheme of Qurʾanic studies.", "reasons": "Suyūṭī says earlier scholars lacked a comparable compilation; al-Kāfījī's short work covered definitions of tafsīr, taʾwīl, Qurʾān, sūra and verse, opinion exegesis conditions, and etiquette. Al-Balqīnī introduced Jalāl al-Dīn's organized Mawāqiʿ al-ʿUlūm. Its divisions include Meccan/Medinan, travel/residence, time and occasion of revelation; mutawātir, solitary and anomalous readings plus transmitters and memorisers; and pauses, beginnings, imāla, lengthening, hamza easing and assimilation."}]}

{"id": "6:95/q01", "question": "Why is the opening assertion emphatic and nominal?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q01/p1", "position": "It affirms God's enduring creative attribute and presses a neglected inference.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says polytheists accepted these acts but ignored their implication for resurrection, so inna addresses a state like doubt; the nominal form conveys an enduring attribute of act or power. He says the sentence is not formally restrictive."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q02", "question": "What does fāliq mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether falq is creation, the planted seed opening into new growth, an existing fissure, or separation from the parent plant.", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q02/p1", "position": "God splits grain and fruit stones so plants and trees emerge.", "reasons": "Qatāda, al-Suddī, Ibn Zayd and many others describe shoots, ears, palms, and trees emerging. Al-Zajjāj stresses dry seed yielding tender green growth. Al-Ṭabarī prefers this because the next clause explains the split; Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds it comprehensive; Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī call it the apparent or majority reading. Rāzī describes shoots rising and roots descending in moist soil. Elmalılı details pressure and cracks."}, {"id": "6:95/q02/p2", "position": "It points to the existing two clefts in a grain or pit.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Abū Mālik identify the visible fissures, sometimes specifying wheat or barley and date stones. Abū Muslim adds their evenness. Al-Ālūsī likens the shape to a cistern narrow above and wide below, but finds it less demonstrative of power; Ibn ʿAṭiyya objects that it arbitrarily narrows the lesson."}, {"id": "6:95/q02/p3", "position": "Fāliq means creator or originator of grain and stones.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil transmit this. Al-Wāḥidī equates it with fāṭir; Rāzī and Ālūsī explain origination figuratively as splitting imagined darkness of nonexistence; Study Quran links the root of Fāṭir. Al-Ṭabarī and Abū Ḥayyān object that Arabic does not attest simple falaqa for create; Samīn cites al-Farrā's synonymy in reply."}, {"id": "6:95/q02/p4", "position": "God splits the grain bearing ear and the fruit bearing the pit.", "reasons": "Ismāʿīl al-Ḍarīr gives this direction of splitting, in contrast with opening a planted kernel."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q03", "question": "What lexical range supports the word fāliq?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q03/p1", "position": "Its root is splitting or separating parts; related senses name things split or openings.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī cites a low place as though split from earth; Samīn lists a hollow between rises, Moses' sea, morning, rivers (27:61), a split thing, a marvel, and gaps among mountains or camel humps (113:1). Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Rāghib give the core sense."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q04", "question": "How is fāliq al-ḥabb constructed grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q04/p1", "position": "It is an active participle in annexation to the grain.", "reasons": "Jishumī says annexation drops nunation and makes al-ḥabb genitive. Samīn says genuine annexation can refer to completed action, supported by ʿAbdallāh's past tense reading; alternatively non-genuine annexation narrates a present or future act, with al-ḥabb genitive in form but accusative in syntactic position. With nunation Jishumī makes it accusative object."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q05", "question": "Is fāliq read as a participle or a past verb?", "turns_on": "Whether the divine action is worded as a participial attribute or a completed finite act.", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q05/p1", "position": "The familiar wording has the active participle fāliq.", "reasons": "Samīn discusses its annexation and its past or ongoing sense."}, {"id": "6:95/q05/p2", "position": "ʿAbdallāh reads falaqa as a past tense verb.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports the reading; Samīn uses it to support taking the annexation of the familiar participle as genuine."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q06", "question": "What does al-ḥabb denote?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q06/p1", "position": "It is the collective or plural for grains and seeds, especially those without fruit stones.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, Elmalılı and Ibn ʿĀshūr give ḥabba as the singular; Muqātil and others list wheat, barley and corn, and al-Kalbī contrasts them with pitted fruit. Elmalılı calls them herb seeds."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q07", "question": "What does al-nawā denote?", "turns_on": "Whether nawā names the familiar fruit stone or the germ within a seed.", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q07/p1", "position": "It denotes the stones or kernels of dates and other fruit.", "reasons": "Muqātil names peaches, jujubes, apricots, grapes, pears; other lists add figs. Al-Layth gives nawāt as singular and a verb for stone formation. Samīn notes collective form, distance as another sense, hardened date pit, and final radical yāʾ. Ālūsī distinguishes common unqualified date use from broader fruit pit use and records variant gender and plurals."}, {"id": "6:95/q07/p2", "position": "The word more aptly denotes the plant germ inside a grain.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reasons that both ḥabb and nawā are plants and compares this germ with the kernel of a date or grape."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q08", "question": "What does splitting seeds show about God's action?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q08/p1", "position": "The coordinated emergence and design of plants reveal God's power, wisdom, provision and singular governance.", "reasons": "Rāzī argues opposite upward and downward growth cannot follow one natural tendency; fragile roots penetrate dense soil, while walnuts, citrons, grapes, leaf veins, fruit arrangements and animal-specific effects show a choosing designer. Biqāʿī relays these examples. Elmalılı notes plant anatomy and diverse structures; Iṣlāḥī notes seed potential and coordinated earth, sky, winds, clouds and seasons; Ālūsī calls it perfect power. Jishumī calls grain and pits signs of provision and fruit. Rāzī traces plant service through animals to human knowledge, love and worship (51:56); leaf contemplation recalls uncountable favors (14:34)."}, {"id": "6:95/q08/p2", "position": "The seed's return from decay is evidence for resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says observed creation establishes ability to raise the dead; Abū Ḥayyān connects the kernel sign with the preceding resurrection discussion (6:94); Iṣlāḥī compares seeds rising from earth after decay with human burial and resurrection."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q09", "question": "What inward meanings are given to the grain and stone?", "turns_on": "Whether the seed image maps to inner moral growth or to believers' and disbelievers' primordial clay.", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q09/p1", "position": "They symbolize contents or capacities of the heart and soul.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says the heart's seed yields sincerity and ostentation; another interpretation says God reveals sincerity and hypocrisy. Qāshānī says spirit light splits the heart's seed into knowledge and gnosis and heart light splits the soul's kernel into virtues. Qāshānī also says God changes people's states, so they should not turn from Him."}, {"id": "6:95/q09/p2", "position": "Grain and kernel symbolize mixed clay of believers and disbelievers.", "reasons": "A report from Abū ʿAbdallāh makes grain believers' loved clay and kernel disbelievers' clay distanced from good; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explicitly labels this inward rather than apparent meaning and defers the clay traditions."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q10", "question": "What are the living and dead brought out of one another?", "turns_on": "Whether living and dead name growth and dryness, literal animal life and inert matter, faith and unbelief, or a comprehensive cycle.", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q10/p1", "position": "Living plants or palms grow from dry seeds or stones, and dry seed or stone comes from living plants.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers this because it follows seed splitting, while allowing the verse's general wording to encompass other examples. Al-Zajjāj and Ṭabrisī cite Arab usage calling upright green growth living and cut or withered growth dead; 30:50 supports it for Kashshāf and Nasafī. Iṣlāḥī includes later yellowing and decay. Ṭabarī, al-Suddī and Abū Mālik supply both directions."}, {"id": "6:95/q10/p2", "position": "Living people or animals emerge from lifeless semen, and semen comes from the living.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and many transmitters give this reciprocal example. Muqātil adds animals; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also mentions birds, fish and other egg-bearing creatures. Jishumī and Ṭabrisī favor literal life; Rāzī says literal life and lifelessness require a wise determiner."}, {"id": "6:95/q10/p3", "position": "Birds or other animals emerge from eggs, and lifeless eggs come from living animals.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima, Abū ʿAlī, al-Jubbāʾī and others use the egg and bird or chicken cycle. Jishumī prefers this with the semen example as literally living versus lifeless. Iṣlāḥī rejects limiting the verse to the egg or hen puzzle."}, {"id": "6:95/q10/p4", "position": "Believers come from disbelievers and disbelievers from believers, with moral reversals too.", "reasons": "ʿUmar, al-Ḥasan and Ibn ʿAbbās are reported. Ibn ʿAbbās names Abraham and Noah's son and extends it to obedience, knowledge and intelligence; a clay tradition explains it through the mixing and separation of believers' and disbelievers' clay (6:122)."}, {"id": "6:95/q10/p5", "position": "An alert, capable person may arise from a dull, helpless person, or conversely.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī adds this as a further possibility; Bursevī's report from Ibn ʿAbbās also contrasts the intelligent with the foolish and the scholar with the ignorant."}, {"id": "6:95/q10/p6", "position": "The clauses state the broad law of life, death and renewal in all creatures.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says their

Ibn ʿĀshūr includes milk, musk, pearls and bezoar stones from living animals."}, {"id": "6:95/q10/p7", "position": "The inner heart alternates between life through spirit and death through desire.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says spirit light can revive the dead soul, while desire can overcome and deaden the living heart. Bursevī sees faith growing from the declaration of oneness and hypocrisy emerging from the same declaration."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q11", "question": "Are plants literally living in this wording?", "turns_on": "Whether 'life' is taken strictly as sentient or animate life or extended to vegetation.", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q11/p1", "position": "Growth may be called life and dry or inert matter death by broad usage or metaphor.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zajjāj cite Arab usage of living upright vegetation; Nasafī invokes revived earth (30:50). Bursevī says literal life requires sensation and voluntary motion, so growth is metaphorical. Ālūsī says applying literal life and death to plants requires a general metaphor or combined senses."}, {"id": "6:95/q11/p2", "position": "Strictly, living means possessing life, so plants are not living.", "reasons": "Rāzī draws the literal boundary; this favors the human and bird examples. Jishumī explicitly ranks person and bird interpretations higher because they are literal; Ṭabrisī calls the semen example soundest."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q12", "question": "What reported incidents apply the life-from-death phrase to people?", "turns_on": "Which woman and episode the reported application concerns.", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q12/p1", "position": "The Prophet applied it to Khālida bint al-Aswad, a righteous woman with an unbelieving father.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits a visit in which the Prophet asks who she is and praises God as the one bringing living from dead; another version supplies her character and father's unbelief."}, {"id": "6:95/q12/p2", "position": "The Prophet recited it for Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqba after her migration.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr records that she migrated to Medina, refused return to the polytheists, and received this figurative application."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q13", "question": "How is the clause 'He brings the living from the dead' parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q13/p1", "position": "It explains the seed splitting, either independently or as another predicate of inna.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Rāzī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and Bayḍāwī say sprouting explains how splitting brings life from dead matter; Samīn supplies the independent and second-predicate parses. Ibn ʿĀshūr favors the unjoined clarifying clause and allows a broader second predicate; Ibn Kathīr says the explanation precedes the next coordinated phrase."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q14", "question": "Why is the living mentioned before the dead?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q14/p1", "position": "The order honors the living.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Ṣāʾigh lists living before dead among examples of precedence for honor, alongside men before women, free before enslaved, and hearing before sight; Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmits al-Naqqāsh on the latter pair."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q15", "question": "Why use a verb for bringing out the living and a participle for the dead?", "turns_on": "Whether the contrast privileges life's renewal over death's stability or jointly conveys recurrence and permanence.", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q15/p1", "position": "The verb depicts renewed action and the more striking, mobile production of life; the participle conveys stable production of death.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir compares recurring divine provision (35:3) with a dog's fixed posture (18:18). Rāzī and the Imam say life is nobler and gets more verbal attention; Biqāʿī calls the participle settled fact. Ibn al-Munīr adds vivid present tense and temporal priority, while Iṣlāḥī stresses God's decision over unavoidable death. Samarrai links movement with life and stillness with death; ʿAlī's examples include 22:63 and 2:15."}, {"id": "6:95/q15/p2", "position": "Both forms together mark the processes as recurring, constant and intrinsic, with neither privileged.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the imperfect as repeated deliberate action rather than coincidence and the participle as permanence; he declines to make one process superior."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q16", "question": "How is al-mayyit read?", "turns_on": "Whether yāʾ is geminated or light in the two occurrences.", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q16/p1", "position": "Nafiʿ, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim double the yāʾ in both occurrences.", "reasons": "Rāzī records this distribution; Nashr says Abū Jaʿfar doubles yāʾ across the listed parallels, including 'the living from the dead and the dead from the living.'"}, {"id": "6:95/q16/p2", "position": "Other readers lighten both occurrences to mayt.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the light form holds consistently for this form elsewhere; Qiraat Er says mayt may suggest recent or less permanent death and is repeated here for internal consistency."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q17", "question": "What does 'bringing the dead from the living' coordinate with?", "turns_on": "Whether syntax follows the matching participles or the paired meanings of life and death.", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q17/p1", "position": "The participle coordinates with fāliq, while the intervening finite clause explains seed splitting.", "reasons": "Kashshāf and its followers align two participial predicates; Zarkashī endorses this because bringing dead from living does not explain seed splitting. Abū Ḥayyān notes noun and verb may still coordinate semantically; Samīn cites al-Zamakhsharī and poetry with mixed forms."}, {"id": "6:95/q17/p2", "position": "It coordinates with the preceding verbal clause as the paired, completing opposite.", "reasons": "Ibn Mālik treats the noun as verbal in sense, and Samīn gives this alternative, citing poems permitting noun and verb coordination. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the semantic pairing and 6:96 analogy; Ibn al-Munīr says the frequent paired present clauses make a syntactic break unlikely. Burhān sets out coordination by overt wording, syntactic position, and supposition."}]}
{"id": "6:95/q18", "question": "What follows from God producing opposite outcomes?", "turns_on": "Whether diverse outcomes imply a freely acting divine governor and how created causes participate in that governance.", "positions": [{"id": "6:95/q18/p1", "position": "Opposite and varied effects point to a wise, freely acting God rather than an independent uniform nature.", "reasons": "Rāzī uses opposed plant growth, diverse fruit qualities and a medicinal counteraction between poison and snakebite; Biqāʿī and Elmalılı likewise reject uniform natural causes. Ibn ʿĀshūr says a free agent can produce opposites; Biqāʿī says fixed intrinsic properties could not. Iṣlāḥī argues a rival god should be able to suspend the universal life-death law; uninterrupted matter or blind force would not explain change."}, {"id": "6:95/q18/p2", "position": "Created causes really act, but continuously depend on God's determination and guidance.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the Qur'an attributes real effects to creatures and presumes regular causation (7:101), while tracing all changing capacities, actions and ends to God (13:16; 39:62; 25:2; 20:50; 87:2-3). He rejects a withdrawn creator, occasionalism, suspended causality in miracles, and origin-only dependence.
